title: ～ようだ — it seems ～, it appears ～
summary: Gives a judgment based on what the speaker has seen, heard or felt: “it seems ～.” It attaches to the plain form of verbs and adjectives, な-adjectives with な, and nouns with の. The tone is a little formal and soft.

patterns.gloss: verbs and い-adjectives: plain form + ようだ

patterns.form: な形容詞 ＋ な／名詞 ＋ の ＋ ようだ
patterns.gloss: 静かなようだ, 病気のようだ

body.p: ようだ is used when the speaker has some evidence from their own senses: 誰もいない (no one answers), みんなコートを着ている (everyone wears a coat), so 外は寒いようだ. The judgment is based on what you observe, not on pure guesswork.

～そうだ (hearsay) passes on what you were told, and ～そうだ (appearance) is based on looks. ～らしい also has a hearsay feel. ようだ is the neutral choice for an inference from direct evidence. The polite form is ようです.

examples.ja: 家（いえ）には誰（だれ）もいないようだ。
examples.romaji: Ie ni wa dare mo inai yō da.
examples.tr: It seems no one is at home.

examples.ja: 外（そと）は寒（さむ）いようだ。みんなコートを着（き）ている。
examples.romaji: Soto wa samui yō da. Minna kōto o kite iru.
examples.tr: It seems cold outside. Everyone is wearing a coat.

examples.ja: 隣（となり）の部屋（へや）には誰（だれ）かいるようです。
examples.romaji: Tonari no heya ni wa dare ka iru yō desu.
examples.tr: It seems someone is in the next room.

pitfalls: Nouns take の and な-adjectives take な before ようだ: 病気のようだ, 静かなようだ.
It is not for things the speaker already knows for sure, such as your own feelings.
